names.value: Te Fatu Moana ("Lord of the Sea")

Marquesan reflex of Proto-Polynesian *Tangaroa (cf. Maori Tangaroa, Tahitian Ta'aroa, Hawaiian Kanaloa); the medial -ng- of Tangaroa is lost in Marquesan, yielding Tanaoa. In the cosmogony the name personifies the primeval Po (darkness/void); the element conveys the boundless dark sea-night out of which light separated.

variants.notes: In a widespread Polynesian (and Marquesan) variant, the first man (Tiki, or Tane in some traditions) forms a woman out of sand/earth and takes her to wife, the woman bearing the name Hina-(tu-na-)one; the union founds mankind. Some Maori traditions; the Raro-Toaga (Cook Islands) tradition has Māui's father and mother both as children of Tangaroa

variants.notes: A minority Maori variant assigns paternity to Tangaroa (the great Polynesian sea-god, called Kanaloa in Hawaiian) instead of Makeatutara, with a mortal woman as mother. The Raro-Toaga (Cook Islands) tradition treats both parents as Tangaroa's children, which would push Māui to fully-divine and fail strict criterion. The dominant Maori (Grey, White, Tregear) tradition is Makeatutara + Taranga, which passes strict.

citations.reference: Hawaiian tradition; Beckwith 1940; Fornander 1878-1885

variants.notes: In the Hawaiian variant, Māui-a-Kalana ("Māui son of Akalana") is one of four Māui-brothers (Māui-Mua, Māui-Waena, Māui-Ki'iki'i, Māui-a-Kalana) born to Akalana (mortal father) and Hina (often divine — moon-goddess in some traditions, mortal in others). The Hawaiian version is therefore a different parental configuration from the Maori dominant tradition.

citations.reference: Mangarevan tradition

variants.notes: In the Mangarevan tradition, Ataraga has eight sons all named Māui (Māui-mua, Māui-muri, Māui-toere-mataroa, Tumei-hauhia, Māui-tikitiki-toga, Māui-matavaru, Māui-taha, Māui-roto). It is Māui-matavaru ("eight-eyed") who is the culture-hero. Different parental configuration again.

names.value: Maori-Polynesian: rata — etymology contested. The name is shared across Polynesian language-traditions with the canonical t↔l↔r consonant-shift (Rata → Laka → Lata). One reading derives the name from a tree-name (the Rata is a Maori tree, Metrosideros), making the name iconographically appropriate for the canoe-builder-hero who must learn the proper tikanga of tree-felling.

names.value: Maori-Polynesian: wahie ("firewood") + roa ("long") — "Long-piece-of-firewood." The name was given by Tāwhaki to commemorate his revival-by-fire-after-cousin-attack: Hinepiripiri had nursed him back to health by feeding the fire with a single huge log; Tāwhaki named their son after this log so that the duty of avenging his father's wrongs would often be recalled by the firewood-name. The canonical-Polynesian instructive-name ("name designed to remind the bearer of the obligation embedded in it") narrative-device.

names.value: Hina the woman in the moon

Proto-Polynesian *Sina 'grey, silvery; the moon', the wide-spread Polynesian moon- and first-woman goddess; the aspect-names: Hina-nui-te-araara 'great Hina the watcher', Hina-i-a'a-i-te-marama 'Hina who stepped into the moon', Hina-fa'auru-va'a 'Hina the canoe-steerer', Hina-tu-a-uta 'Hina standing inland' — Henry, Ancient Tahiti (1928)

sources.claim: Te Moana ('the Ocean') is the Tokelauan sea-god, son of the supreme god Tui Tokelau and second in rank, who manifests in the waterspout and was called upon to raise destructive waves and winds against attackers of Fakaofo.

sources.claim: 'Aho'eitu, son of the sky-god Tangaloa 'Eitumatupu'a and the mortal 'Ilaheva (Va'epopua), is the first Tu'i Tonga (sacred paramount) of divine descent: climbing the toa tree to the sky to find his father, he was killed and eaten by his jealous sky-brothers and then resurrected when Tangaloa made them disgorge his body into a kumete bowl, after which he was sent down to rule Tonga, his eldest brother becoming the Tu'i Faleua and the other four the Falefa.

citations.reference: Gifford, E. W. Tongan Myths and Tales (Bishop Museum Bulletin 8, 1924)
Collocott, E. E. V. Tales and Poems of Tonga (Bishop Museum Bulletin 46, 1928)

sources.claim: Ahoeitu, son of Ilaheva and Tangaloa Eitumatupua, climbs to the sky and is killed by his jealous brothers. His father directs the recovery of his remains and his return to life. He returns to earth as the first Tu‘i Tonga of divine descent, displacing an earlier worm-descended line.

names.value: Tongan; the element hiku means 'tail, tip, end' — consonant with the deity's defining long tail. A full secure gloss of the whole name is not established; only the hiku element is given.

relations.subject: tongan_hikuleo

sources.reference: Gifford, E. W. Tongan Myths and Tales (Bishop Museum Bulletin 8, 1924), on Hikule'o, Tangaloa and Maui dividing the cosmos as the children of Taufulifonua

relations.notes: Hikule'o and Maui (Motu'a) are siblings of the cosmos-dividing generation, children of Taufulifonua; Maui below holds one end of the cord that restrains Hikule'o's tail.

sources.reference: E. W. Gifford, Tongan Myths and Tales (1924), pp. 19
E. W. Gifford, Tongan Myths and Tales (1924), pp. 19

sources.claim: Hikule'o (gender variable in the sources — male in Mariner and some tellings, 'the goddess of Pulotu' in others) is the Tongan deity who keeps Pulotu, the western spirit-land of the dead and of the gods, and holds the fertility of the land; the deity has a great tail that must be held by a cord — one end with Tangaloa in the sky, the other with Maui below — lest, coming forth, the land and the living be drawn after the dead into Pulotu.

Collocott, E. E. V. Tales and Poems of Tonga (Bishop Museum Bulletin 46, 1928)

names.value: 'Ilaheva, personal name; Va'epopua is a by-name from her place, Popua (she is 'Ilaheva of Va'epopua). The mortal mother of 'Aho'eitu.

relations.subject: tongan_ilaheva

sources.reference: Gifford, E. W. Tongan Myths and Tales (Bishop Museum Bulletin 8, 1924), on 'Ilaheva as wife of Tangaloa 'Eitumatupu'a

relations.notes: Wife on earth of the sky-god; mother of 'Aho'eitu.

sources.claim: 'Ilaheva, called Va'epopua for her home at Popua, is the mortal Tongan woman of the older, autochthonous population whom the sky-god Tangaloa 'Eitumatupu'a took to wife and who bore 'Aho'eitu, the first Tu'i Tonga, later showing him the toa tree by which to climb to his divine father.

citations.reference: Gifford, E. W. Tongan Myths and Tales (Bishop Museum Bulletin 8, 1924)
Collocott, E. E. V. Tales and Poems of Tonga (Bishop Museum Bulletin 46, 1928)

sources.claim: Ilaheva, also called Vaepopua, meets Tangaloa Eitumatupua while fishing. She raises their son Ahoeitu at Popua and later shows him the casuarina route to his father in the sky. The Reiter–Baker passage does not name her parents.

citations.reference: E. W. Gifford, Tongan Myths and Tales (1924), Reiter–Baker account, pp. 25–27

sources.claim: Tangaloa 'Eitumatupu'a is the Tongan sky-god — one of the four sons of Tangaloa in the heavens — who descended to Tongatapu on a great toa (casuarina/ironwood) tree, took the mortal woman 'Ilaheva (Va'epopua) to wife, and fathered 'Aho'eitu, whom he made the first Tu'i Tonga of divine descent, so founding the sacred paramountcy of Tonga.

citations.reference: Gifford, E. W. Tongan Myths and Tales (Bishop Museum Bulletin 8, 1924)
Collocott, E. E. V. 'Notes on Tongan Religion', Journal of the Polynesian Society 30 (1921)

sources.claim: Tangaloa Eitumatupua descends by a casuarina tree and fathers Ahoeitu with Ilaheva. After Ahoeitu’s heavenly brothers kill him, Eitumatupua directs his restoration and appoints him to rule Tonga. Gifford’s collected accounts distinguish this figure from other named Tangaloa.

discoveries.name: Iku, Tapairu, Toa, Mahuta; five unnamed daughters
discoveries.issue: Named records and source-specific relationships authored; five daughters and the immediate parentage of Mahuta remain unnamed in the passage.

discoveries.name: Te-aka-ia-Roe, Te-tangaengae / Te-vaerua, Te-manava-roa
discoveries.issue: Named figures and source-specific relationships authored. The two Te-manava-roa figures remain explicitly distinct.

discoveries.name: Mauike, Ra, Tekea, Ngana
discoveries.issue: Named figures and source-specific relationships authored. The two Te-manava-roa figures remain explicitly distinct.

discoveries.name: Haumea and her named family accounts
discoveries.issue: Immediate Kanaloa, Kane, Papa, Wakea, Ku-hele-i-po and Mapunaia-aala relationships authored. Kumulipo Fifteenth Era spouses and explicit grandson relationships authored without invented intermediate parents. Other named branches remain under review.

discoveries.name: Hina-a-rauriki, Rogo-tumu-here
discoveries.issue: Named records and explicit wife, abductor and rescuer relationships authored.

discoveries.name: Manufili
discoveries.issue: Named carpenter and helper relationship authored.

discoveries.name: Twenty-three Malietoa generations after Savea
discoveries.issue: Source reports count but does not name intermediate generations. No invented parent-child chain to Malietoa Talavou.

discoveries.name: Tarauri’s unnamed brother; Tangiia’s unnamed sister; Lu’s unnamed father
discoveries.issue: Relationships are reported in source descriptions; no fabricated personal names or IDs.

discoveries.name: Liliuokalani Fourteenth Era: Kahiko / Kahikoluamea, Kupulauakehau, Kulaniehu, Koiaakalani, Hina variants; preceding husband/wife table
discoveries.issue: All preceding spouse pairs are authored as explicitly seeded textual branches, without invented parentage between rows. Wakea’s named parents and Hinakaweoa are authored. Kulaniehu, Koiaakalani and the other Hina forms still need identity decisions.

discoveries.name: Liliuokalani Fifteenth Era: Ole, Pupue, Kamahele, Manaku, Hikohoale, Kahiko, Kaea, Luakahakona, Koulamaikalani, Luanuu, Kawaomaaukele, Kii, Hinakoula, Ulu, Nanaulu, Punuu, Nana, Kapulani, Nanaie, Kahaumokuleia, Nanaielani, Hinakinau, Waikalani, Kekauilani, Kuheleimoana, Mapuuaiaaala, Konohiki, Hakaululena, Waolena, Mahuie, Akalana, Hinaakeahi, four Maui, Kialoa, Kiaakapoko, Pimoe, Mahanauluehu, Hinakeka, Peapea, Moemoe
discoveries.issue: All listed spouses, Ole, Nanaulu, Akalana/Hinaakeahi, the four Maui and named narrative figures are authored. Textual spouse-pair branches enter the audit as explicit seeds; no connecting parent edges were inferred from their order. Comparison with Fornander’s explicit child columns is separately recorded below.

discoveries.name: Fornander island genealogy: Kuluwaiea, Hinanuiakalana/Hinanuialana, Kaulawahine, Hina, Lua, Walinuu, Keaukanai, Uluhina; personified island births
discoveries.source: Fornander first series (1916), Formation and Origin, chs. I–IV
discoveries.issue: Named partners and twelve personified islands are authored with competing cited accounts. Molokini’s afterbirth origin is represented without inventing human parentage. The tentative Haumea/Kuluwaiea interpretation is qualified.

discoveries.name: Piki, Havea Lolofonua, Maui Loa, Maui Puku; named Tangaloa; Takataka and Lomu genealogies
discoveries.issue: Separate records, group records and selectable competing parentages authored. Maatu, Takataka, Collocott as reported by Gifford, and Lomu are not combined.

discoveries.name: Te-more-tu; Te Anu-matao and four fish-class children; Māori Tinirau; Tui Tokelau
discoveries.issue: Named parent and descendant records and source-specific accounts authored; Tokelauan counterpart added. Six of nine Rua daughters are unnamed in this entry; Rua-te-pupuke, Rua-te-hihiko, Rua-te-mahara still require source-specific identity review.

discoveries.name: Sinaleana, Sina of Manu’a, unnamed king of Manu’a; Ariari; Tubo; Vaka-akau-uli
discoveries.issue: Named Samoan branch implemented from Turner XXI. Ariari and cosmical Fe’e implemented from Turner I §§6,8; Tapuaau from IV §8. Tubo and Vaka-akau-uli belong to a separately qualified Tongan Tagaloa context from Tregear. Unnamed partners remain unnamed.

discoveries.name: Tuanui-ka-rere and Tangiia-ka-rere (Mangaian eclipse figures)
discoveries.issue: Corrected the earlier working-note attribution to Atiu. Gill explicitly contrasts Mangaian demons with Rarotongan Tangaroa. Distinct records carry functional comparison, without equating Tuamotuan or other Tangiia figures.

discoveries.name: Disputed Fornander/Lawson cosmogony; Tanaoa, Mutuhei, Atea, Ono, Atanua
discoveries.issue: Descriptions and lifecycle claims now explicitly carry Handy’s authenticity objection. No genealogy or identity is silently deleted.

discoveries.name: Fe’e local cult forms; unnamed Savaii spouse and Upolu chief; Fale
discoveries.issue: The spouse and her father are not personally named. Fale appears as the first-person speaker in the quoted priestly prayer, without enough information to establish a separate biographical record. Local cult contexts are not assigned the cosmical cuttlefish’s parents.

discoveries.name: Fornander’s explicit ancestral tables: Hoohokukalani; Kamole; Hai/Kai; Ulukou; Nanamea; Kapunui/Kapunuu; Hinakawea; Mauiakalana; Hinakealohaila; descendants through Kamehameha; earlier ancestors of Kahiko and Papa
discoveries.source: Fornander first series (1916), Formation/Origin ch. VI and History of Kualii ch. IV
discoveries.issue: Named rows now have explicit targets and independent accounts; bracketed groups remain qualified and uncertain cross-text identities remain disputed.

discoveries.name: Kaulu, Kaeha, Makalii and Maoleha nets; Haumea’s death at Niuhelewai
discoveries.source: Fornander first series (1916), Story of Kaulu
discoveries.issue: Complete Legend of Kaulu reviewed; named family and participants, cited objects and source-specific lifecycle events authored.

discoveries.name: Fornander named genealogical tables through Kamehameha and alternative Oahu ancestry
discoveries.source: Fornander Collection (1916), Formation and Origin VI; History of Kualii IV
discoveries.issue: All reviewed rows have explicit IDs and selectable source-specific accounts. Repeated names remain distinct across generations; braced father groups remain unresolved as individual paternity. Wider narrative enrichment is not certified.

discoveries.name: Hakaukahi and Limapaihala; unnamed mate of Kolea, unnamed second net and unnamed attacking spirits
discoveries.source: Fornander Collection, first series (1916), Legend of Kaulu, opening family, heavenly encounters and return to Kailua; notes 735–745
discoveries.issue: Hakaukahi and Limapaihala name Kaulu’s speaking right and left hands, not independently identified ancestors. The other participants or object remain unnamed; no personal names or genealogies are invented.

discoveries.name: Differently spelled Kumulipo and Fornander genealogy entries
discoveries.source: Fornander Collection, first series (1916), Formation and Origin VI and History of Kualii IV, named genealogical columns
discoveries.issue: Thirty-two comparisons retain separate records and explicit targeted-disputed Names links. Corresponding table positions alone do not establish identical individuals or transfer families.

discoveries.name: Six unnamed daughters of Tangaroa; Ruatepupuke’s unnamed intermediate ancestor and grandson
discoveries.source: Edward Tregear, Maori-Polynesian Comparative Dictionary (1891), pp. 463–464, Tangaroa entry; Brett Graham, Whakairo – Māori carving (2017), Legendary origins of carving, East Coast account
discoveries.issue: The reviewed sources give counts or relationships without these personal names. No intermediate parent or invented child is supplied.

discoveries.name: Hingaangaroa, Tūkākī and Iwirākau; Te Rāwheoro
discoveries.source: Brett Graham, Whakairo – Māori carving (2017), Legendary origins of carving, East Coast account
discoveries.issue: The cited page places these people and the school in the later history of carving, not as identified family members of the named divine network. Historical transmission context is recorded here; no genealogical link is inferred.

discoveries.name: Hawaiian Maui regional families: Hin-alau-ae, Hina, Makalii, Nu-lo-hiki, Pu‘upehe, Kapokoholua, Kapoiliili, Pua-iki, Kumulama, Ku-olo-kele, Limaloa, Luehu, Uniho-kahi and Ka-alae-nui-a-hina
discoveries.issue: Passages read; regional accounts and named family branches require record authoring and explicit identity review.

discoveries.name: Kumu-honua/Kane-la‘a-uli, Lalohonua, Ka-mai-eli; Nu‘u, Lua-nu‘u/Kane-hoa-lani, Hawaii-loa, Eleeleua-lani; Ahukai, Wela-ahi-lani-nui, Owe, La‘ila‘i and Kumulipo founders
discoveries.issue: Genealogical commentary read. Christian reinterpretation and source-specific lineages must be distinguished before additional accounts are authored.

discoveries.name: Tuamotuan Maui: Ataraga, Huahega, Mahuike, Hina, Tuna, Peka-nui, Ri, Togio, Rori-tau, Tupa, Dawn-maid and Maid-of-the-Moon; Rarotongan Iro-ma-oata, Moe-tara-uri, Akimano and Pou-ariki
discoveries.issue: Named comparative branches discovered; existing records and specific accounts need continued review, without transplanting Hawaiian genealogy.

discoveries.name: Tangaroa-whakamau-tai; internal etymology and reconstructed Polynesian form
discoveries.source: Legacy Best/POLLEX citations; Tregear Tangaroa entry
discoveries.issue: The reviewed passages do not verify these assertions. Previous public claims are preserved in correction history; direct Best and POLLEX passage verification remains necessary.
